Reading to Write: Say-Mean-Matter

🖼️ Framing Our Work

One way to cultivate literacy routines in our classrooms is to help students move beyond surface understanding and into deeper thinking about texts.

Building on the habits of daily writing and entering conversations with They Say / I Say, the Say-Mean-Matter framework offers students a scaffold for analysis/commentary. By breaking the process into three simple moves—what the text says, what it means, and why it matters—students learn to slow down, engage with ideas more thoughtfully, and consider significance.

Equally important, Say-Mean-Matter provides a flexible tool students can use across texts and disciplines, giving them a consistent routine for making meaning and connecting their reading to bigger questions in school and in life.

📝What to Expect

In this module, you will:

✅ Explore the Say-Mean-Matter framework as a way to help students move beyond summary to deeper analysis and commentary.

✅ Practice using Say-Mean-Matter with quotes and short excerpts as an entry point into the routine.

✅ Participate in the Say-Mean-Matter discussion by sharing your own three-part response and reflections, and engaging with other teachers’ posts.

✅ Earn the Say-Mean-Matter microcredential by reflecting with your facilitator on how you will introduce this routine, creating a classroom-ready example, and identifying which strategy you’ll try out in Module 4.

🧭 Explore and Learn

Say–Mean–Matter

In Deeper Reading, Kelly Gallagher introduces the Say-Mean-Matter framework as a way to push students beyond summary toward analysis and significance. The strategy invites students to work with a short excerpt, quote, or passage, and respond in three parts:

  • Say: What does the text literally say? (Paraphrase or summarize the excerpt in your own words.)

  • Mean: What does this text mean? (Interpret the author’s ideas, explore implications, or explain the underlying message.)

  • Matter: Why does this matter? (Connect the excerpt to broader themes, issues, or contexts; explain its significance for readers or the world.)

This simple framework helps students practice analysis in manageable steps. It can be used in Writer’s Notebooks for quick responses, in small group or partner discussions, or as a scaffold for longer written responses. Over time, Say-Mean-Matter builds students’ capacity to see beyond what a text says on the surface and consider its deeper meaning and relevance.

Say-Mean-Matter with Quotes and Excerpts

The slideshow below provides examples of how to use Say–Mean–Matter with famous quotations, along with a range of examples of students' Say-Mean-Matter responses.Rather than starting with a full text, using quotations or even images (like in Module Two) can be an easy entry point into using Say–Mean–Matter in your classroom.


Using a graphic organizer can help students gather textual evidence and organize their thinking. Click here to make a copy of this resource, which includes a blank graphic organizer as well as a version with helpful They Say / I Say sentence templates for classroom use.

Note that you can also just have students create their own Say-Mean-Matter chart in their Writer's Notebook for quick practice.


💬 Try and Share

Let's try it out! Choose a quote from the slideshow above (or another quote you find) and practice working through the three steps in your Writer’s Notebook, or using the graphic organizer:

  • Say: What does the text literally say?

  • Mean: What does the text mean? How can you interpret or explain it in your own words?

  • Matter: Why does this matter? How does it connect to larger ideas, issues, or contexts?

Once you’ve completed your response, post in the Say-Mean-Matter discussion by sharing your quote/excerpt and your three-part response. Then, reflect on the process:

  • What was it like to try out Say-Mean-Matter?

  • How did the steps shape or extend your thinking about the text?

Finally, take a few minutes to respond to at least two other teachers’ posts to continue the conversation.

🏅 Earn Recognition

The Say-Mean-Matter discussion badge is automatically awarded when you post to the discussion and respond to 2 other posts in the discussion.

The important thing is not to stop questioning. -Albert Einstein Say: Question everything; don't just blindly accept what is presented. Mean: Einstein emphasizes the need for curiosity and continual learning. Instead of accepting things as settled, questioning challenges assumptions and fosters new ideas. Matter: Questioning matters because it leads people to new knowledge and solutions. Questioning also helps develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Questioning challenges existing ideas and helps to improve them. Reflections: This process was very insightful. I was forced to really read for content regarding the quote. It also made me slow down and really dissect what the author was trying to say, and why it was important, and how it connects to the world around me. (I had to realize it was not ALL about me!)

Say: "None of us is as smart as all of us." by Ken Blanchard. Mean: It means that teamwork and collaboration bring out better ideas and solutions than one person can create alone. When people share their thoughts, experiences, and skills, they become strong and smarter together. Matter: This matters because it shows the importance of cooperation in school, work, and life. Reflection: This helped me to slow down and really think about what the quote was saying, instead of just agreeing with it. I had to explain it in my own words and think about why it's important. It made understanding the message clearer and more meaningful. The steps helped me move from just reading the quote to actually analyzing it. "Say" helped me to focus on what the words literally mean. "Mean" pushed me to interpret it, and "Matter" made me connect it to real life and bigger ideas. It showed me that teamwork isn't just about working together but about how combining people's ideas can make a stronger outcome.

Ken Blanchard said, “None of us is as smart as all of us.” This means that we are always better as a community. It’s the same idea as “two heads are better than one.” It is important to remember that, while one person can do a lot, we can do more if we collaborate and work together. More ideas and better ideas can emerge and we can build off of each other.

Again, this felt natural to me. These are things I do without really thinking about the moves I am making. I teach quote sandwiches to help students integrate quotes, so I know I have said just about the same as this (explain your quote, what does it mean? Why does it matter?) but I’ve never thought about framing it like this with the sentence templates and the graphic organizer.

It helps you elaborate. It helps you think about how far you can take the explanation. Instead of stopping with the first part, I’m able to continue and extend my thinking. I can always go back and revise. It’s easier to delete than to not have enough to say. This gives me the chance to find the more to say.

Say: "None of us is as smart as all of us." - Ken Blanchard

Mean: One person isn't as smart as a group of people working together.

Matter: It matters because working with and communicating with others is a large part of life. It's also important because different people bring their own perspectives to solving a problem. and allows people to "experience" a viewpoint different from their own and to build off of each other's views. This is very much like when we have students "Turn and Talk" with each other to discuss their views and answer on a text with each other.

Reflection: It was interesting and made me think of my paraphrasing/using research unit. This would allow for students to not only explain information in their own words but to begin to interpret it (not just regurgitate it).

The steps made me go beyond paraphrasing to interpreting why the quote maters. This could be a great tool to teach interpreting text for researched writing.

Choose a quote or short excerpt from the slideshow in this module and practice working through the three steps in your Writer’s Notebook, or using the graphic organizer:

  • Say: What does the text literally say?

    “None of us is as smart as all of us.” ~Ken Blanchard, American Author

  • Mean: What does the text mean? How can you interpret or explain it in your own words?

    This means that when working on a problem or an issue, you alone may not have the best idea or all of the knowledge required to fix the problem. Relying on others and allowing others to help is beneficial because they may have some kind of knowledge or skill set that would either be a better way to solve the issue, or have more working knowledge of how to fix the issue.

  • Matter: Why does this matter? How does it connect to larger ideas, issues, or contexts?

    This matters not only because it could make your life easier, but it also adds value to the skills and knowledge of others. This connects to larger ideas or issues because it implies that we all have value, we all have knowledge and ideas, and we should not only listen to and value the ideas of others, but it also shows that people need each other to function and flow.

Once you’ve completed your response, post in the Say-Mean-Matter discussion by sharing your quote/excerpt and your three-part response. Then, reflect on the process:

  • What was it like to try out Say-Mean-Matter?

    Trying this strategy was easy for mean. Breaking texts down into what it means is the only way I can understand a lot of what I need to read. I can't just take a text at face value, but have to dig deeper and look for multiple or "hidden" meanings. Instantly when I was doing this, I thought of several ways it could be used/implemented into my current and upcoming units.

  • How did the steps shape or extend your thinking about the text?

    By breaking down what a text literally says you gain a deeper knowledge of what is actually being said and often create a deeper connection to the text. This gives real meaning to text passages and, if guided correctly, can help students extend their understanding and create deeper connections with texts.

Choose a quote or short excerpt from the slideshow in this module and practice working through the three steps in your Writer’s Notebook, or using the graphic organizer:

  • Say: What does the text literally say?

    “None of us is as smart as all of us.” ~Ken Blanchard, American Author

  • Mean: What does the text mean? How can you interpret or explain it in your own words?

    This means that when working on a problem or an issue, you alone may not have the best idea or all of the knowledge required to fix the problem. Relying on others and allowing others to help is beneficial because they may have some kind of knowledge or skill set that would either be a better way to solve the issue, or have more working knowledge of how to fix the issue.

  • Matter: Why does this matter? How does it connect to larger ideas, issues, or contexts?

    This matters not only because it could make your life easier, but it also adds value to the skills and knowledge of others. This connects to larger ideas or issues because it implies that we all have value, we all have knowledge and ideas, and we should not only listen to and value the ideas of others, but it also shows that people need each other to function and flow.

Once you’ve completed your response, post in the Say-Mean-Matter discussion by sharing your quote/excerpt and your three-part response. Then, reflect on the process:

  • What was it like to try out Say-Mean-Matter?

    Trying this strategy was easy for mean. Breaking texts down into what it means is the only way I can understand a lot of what I need to read. I can't just take a text at face value, but have to dig deeper and look for multiple or "hidden" meanings. Instantly when I was doing this, I thought of several ways it could be used/implemented into my current and upcoming units.

  • How did the steps shape or extend your thinking about the text?

    By breaking down what a text literally says you gain a deeper knowledge of what is actually being said and often create a deeper connection to the text. This gives real meaning to text passages and, if guided correctly, can help students extend their understanding and create deeper connections with texts.

You make a great point about deeper connections. The "What does it matter?" section helps students connect a text to a bigger world (ideas, events, etc) that has meaning for the students. When students make connections between their lives and the text, the text takes on greater significance.

  • Says: "One accurate measurement is worth a thousand expert opinions." -Grace Hopper

  • Means: It's is more useful to reflect based on observable data, rather than submit to the opinions of experts.

  • Matters: Many times in education, we are guilty of labeling students based on surface level observations, often based on behavior rather than academic performance. Grace Hopper advices us to look at their performance by evaluating the work they produce. I feel that I can better judge a student's level of understanding from a RACE paragraph compared to a test. Additionally, it is important that we scrutinize our evaluation tools (learning targets and scoring guides) to make sure we are taking accurate measurements.

  • I use Says-Means-Matters multiple times in my class to break down primary sources from the past. Practicing this strategy as the student helped to remind me that it does take more time. Whereas They Say/I Say invites the reader to respond, Says/Means/Matters requires us to go one step further and evaluate the text.

  • The extra step of describing why the text matters forced me to really stop and think about the message. It also encourages the reader to look for ways to apply the meaning to a broader academic discussion.

SAY-MEAN-MATTER RESPONSE

Robert Hunter wrote these lyrics in the Grateful Dead's "Scarlet Begonias": Once in a while you get shown the light in the strangest of places if you look at it right. Hunter meant that we can experience an epiphany or revelation in unexpected ways if we are open to it. If you take these words to heart, you can begin to look at life in new ways. People you may not normally associate with, places you might not normally go, flowers you may not proverbially stop to small--all of these things offer a chance for enlightenment if we are willing to consider what we might be learning from them.

SAY-MEAN-MATTER REFLECTION

When I was beginning the "What does it mean?" section of my response, my brain started exploding with a million things to say. I sifted through my thoughts and realized that my brain was mixing some "What does it matter?" with "What does it mean?" and it reminded me of student papers I've read—papers where they don't stop to sift their thoughts as I did, and they just write it down as they think it.

I suppose, then, that a framework like Say-Mean-Matter helps students organize their thinking. Additionally, this strategy makes you think deeply. I actually could have taken "What does it matter?" section and elaborated. Such a small phrase as that has a lot of weight, especially if you could add the 5 Whys (like with Root Cause Analysis). Why does that matter? And why does THAT matter? And why does THAT matter? ... A lot of thinking involved in that.

Angie, I appreciate your reflection about how your mind wanted to mix together the means and the matters thinking. As a teacher, it is useful to anticipate some of these tripping points and preload instruction around them.

Say-Mean-Matter

*Quote:  “The important thing is not to stop questioning.”  by Albert Einstein

SAY: This quote suggests that curiosity and questioning are essential to learning and discovery.  Einstein emphasizes that, regardless of the obstacles we face, we should always continue to seek understanding and explore new ideas.  

MEAN:  This quote highlights the value of curiosity and critical thinking.  Einstein is telling us that asking questions is crucial for growth, whether it’s in our personal lives or in our studies.  By questioning the world around us, we not only learn more, but we also develop a deeper understanding of how things work.  **I asked my granddaughter - she is in Kindergarten- what she thought it meant, and she said, “It means it’s good to ask things when we don’t know.  I always tell Gritt (her brother) to make sure to raise his hand and ask his teacher a question if he doesn’t know something.  I have the smartest teacher, because she always knows the answer to everything I ask her!”  

MATTER:  This quote matters because it reminds us that curiosity drives progress.  In the classroom, it encourages the students to engage with the material and ask deeper questions rather than just memorizing facts.  It also teaches us that mistakes or confusion are part of the learning process, and they shouldn’t discourage us from seeking answers.  

*Granddaughter–”It matters because then we learn new stuff that we didn’t know.”  

*I absolutely LOVE this strategy.  There are so many ways that it can be used in a classroom, and it definitely requires students to dive deeper into their learning.  It was especially fun to try out on my granddaughter.  Later that day, we were collecting leaves in order to make a “turkey feather” outfit for her to wear on Thanksgiving, and she picked a leaf up and asked me what I saw!  I then asked her what those things were telling her (the leaf was brown/green, there were some lines on it, and it was the size of her hand).  We discussed all kinds of things, along with why all of those things mattered!  

The thought process behind this strategy lends itself to a bigger picture of understanding.    It seems so simple, and is easy enough for a kindergartener to use, yet it provides that deeper level that is crucial to learning.

Say-Mean-Matter

*Quote:  “The important thing is not to stop questioning.”  by Albert Einstein

SAY: This quote suggests that curiosity and questioning are essential to learning and discovery.  Einstein emphasizes that, regardless of the obstacles we face, we should always continue to seek understanding and explore new ideas.  

MEAN:  This quote highlights the value of curiosity and critical thinking.  Einstein is telling us that asking questions is crucial for growth, whether it’s in our personal lives or in our studies.  By questioning the world around us, we not only learn more, but we also develop a deeper understanding of how things work.  **I asked my granddaughter - she is in Kindergarten- what she thought it meant, and she said, “It means it’s good to ask things when we don’t know.  I always tell Gritt (her brother) to make sure to raise his hand and ask his teacher a question if he doesn’t know something.  I have the smartest teacher, because she always knows the answer to everything I ask her!”  

MATTER:  This quote matters because it reminds us that curiosity drives progress.  In the classroom, it encourages the students to engage with the material and ask deeper questions rather than just memorizing facts.  It also teaches us that mistakes or confusion are part of the learning process, and they shouldn’t discourage us from seeking answers.  

*Granddaughter–”It matters because then we learn new stuff that we didn’t know.”  

*I absolutely LOVE this strategy.  There are so many ways that it can be used in a classroom, and it definitely requires students to dive deeper into their learning.  It was especially fun to try out on my granddaughter.  Later that day, we were collecting leaves in order to make a “turkey feather” outfit for her to wear on Thanksgiving, and she picked a leaf up and asked me what I saw!  I then asked her what those things were telling her (the leaf was brown/green, there were some lines on it, and it was the size of her hand).  We discussed all kinds of things, along with why all of those things mattered!  

The thought process behind this strategy lends itself to a bigger picture of understanding.    It seems so simple, and is easy enough for a kindergartener to use, yet it provides that deeper level that is crucial to learning. 

I love the way you made these connections with your grandkids! That's real proof that these strategies can be adapted for multiple grade levels and subjects. Teaching young children to look for deep meaning is setting them up for success, in my opinion. It would be interesting (and fun) to use these strategies in simplified version with children's books, even with older students.

  • Says: "One accurate measurement is worth a thousand expert opinions." -Grace Hopper

  • Means: It's is more useful to reflect based on observable data, rather than submit to the opinions of experts.

  • Matters: Many times in education, we are guilty of labeling students based on surface level observations, often based on behavior rather than academic performance. Grace Hopper advices us to look at their performance by evaluating the work they produce. I feel that I can better judge a student's level of understanding from a RACE paragraph compared to a test. Additionally, it is important that we scrutinize our evaluation tools (learning targets and scoring guides) to make sure we are taking accurate measurements.

  • I use Says-Means-Matters multiple times in my class to break down primary sources from the past. Practicing this strategy as the student helped to remind me that it does take more time. Whereas They Say/I Say invites the reader to respond, Says/Means/Matters requires us to go one step further and evaluate the text.

  • The extra step of describing why the text matters forced me to really stop and think about the message. It also encourages the reader to look for ways to apply the meaning to a broader academic discussion.

Choose a quote from the slideshow above (or another quote you find) and practice working through the three steps in your Writer’s Notebook, or using the graphic organizer:

Say“None of us is as smart as all of us.” 

Ken Blanchard American Author

Say: What does the text literally say?

The text says: None of us is as smart as all of us.

Mean: What does the text mean? How can you interpret or explain it in your own words?

The text means that if we come together as a group, we are smarter than an individual.  We are not smarter than if we were in a group.  We can put all of our thoughts and ideas together, which is better than one person’s thoughts and ideas.

Matter: Why does this matter? How does it connect to larger ideas, issues, or contexts?

I think this quote matters because, whether we are in a school setting or a work setting, it’s better to put everyone’s ideas together than just using an individual’s ideas.  We are better off if we collaborate together than if we make decisions based on one individual.

Once you’ve completed your response, post in the Say-Mean-Matter discussion by sharing your quote/excerpt and your three-part response. Then, reflect on the process:

How did the steps shape or extend your thinking about the text?

I thought about the quote in a real-world setting.  I tried to apply it to many things to justify my thoughts.

I agree that this strategy leads to valuable real world connections. Students often narrow their focus to the words on the page and fail to make meaningful connections to other contexts.

Say: "Anyone who stops learning is old, whether at twenty or eighty. Anyone who keeps learning stays young.". Mean: It is saying that age isn’t about how old you are it’s about your mindset. But if a person keeps learning, growing, and staying curious, they stay “young” because their mind remains active and open. Adam Rich

  • Says: "One accurate measurement is worth a thousand expert opinions." -Grace Hopper

  • Means: It's is more useful to reflect based on observable data, rather than submit to the opinions of experts.

  • Matters: Many times in education, we are guilty of labeling students based on surface level observations, often based on behavior rather than academic performance. Grace Hopper advices us to look at their performance by evaluating the work they produce. I feel that I can better judge a student's level of understanding from a RACE paragraph compared to a test. Additionally, it is important that we scrutinize our evaluation tools (learning targets and scoring guides) to make sure we are taking accurate measurements.

  • I use Says-Means-Matters multiple times in my class to break down primary sources from the past. Practicing this strategy as the student helped to remind me that it does take more time. Whereas They Say/I Say invites the reader to respond, Says/Means/Matters requires us to go one step further and evaluate the text.

  • The extra step of describing why the text matters forced me to really stop and think about the message. It also encourages the reader to look for ways to apply the meaning to a broader academic discussion.

Choose a quote or short excerpt from the slideshow in this module and practice working through the three steps in your Writer’s Notebook, or using the graphic organizer:

  • Say: What does the text literally say?

  • Mean: What does the text mean? How can you interpret or explain it in your own words?

  • Matter: Why does this matter? How does it connect to larger ideas, issues, or contexts?

Once you’ve completed your response, post in the Say-Mean-Matter discussion by sharing your quote/excerpt and your three-part response. Then, reflect on the process:

  • What was it like to try out Say-Mean-Matter?

  • How did the steps shape or extend your thinking about the text?

I am currently using this strategy on a weekly basis with one of the college literarure classes I am teaching. Students are required to read essays and then find quotes that stand out and follow the say/mean/matter process. We then share the quotes and have discussions over the quotes they have chosen. This process has enabled students to engage on a level much deeper than a regular discussion regarding an essay by Orwell, or Emerson. I absolutely love this strategy.
